Six fae in scarlet petal-silk strung along an overhanging alder root, legs dangling, three screaming at the hull below and one already dangling by one knee having bet her hazelnut stake on the wrong boat entirely, a water-vole watching from the root-end with its paws folded.

A knot of fae in moss-velvet crowded onto a mossy boulder mid-stream, two holding a third by the ankles as she leans screaming over the drop, a fat frog sitting steady below absorbing the noise, one fae quietly moving pebbles along a twig to count hulls through.

Fae in marigold leaf-cloth running flat out along the low bank-root keeping level with the leaders, one already waist-deep and laughing, a second wringing out her soaked grass-cord sash as she runs, a kingfisher on the far stone watching the whole spectacle for its own reasons.

Four fae in woven grass perched on a beached oak leaf wide as the whole gravel spit, all facing the wrong bend and cheering a hull already swamped, one fae on a frog's back paddling hard into the current for a better view.

A loose diagonal of dragonflies flying escort above the field, each carrying one fae in plum petal-silk clutching the thorax with both fists, the rearmost fae leaning sideways at a dangerous angle to shout something back at the bank.

Seven fae in berry-red moss-velvet strung out along a fallen branch crossing the whole channel, one lying flat reaching a fern frond down to fend a hull off a stone, a snail making steady progress along the branch toward the far bank and winning.

Fae in birch-bark cloaks crowded into the fork of a bankside root above the first bend, two betting hazelnuts into an upturned acorn cap, one shouting corrections nobody asked for, a newt hanging motionless in the water below watching the same bend for different reasons.

Three fae in copper-thread grass-weave riding the backs of frogs in the shallows, leaning forward with their wings fanned for balance, one frog making a sudden lunge at a mayfly and nearly tipping its rider headfirst into the stream.

A row of fae in cream petal-silk lying flat on a low fern frond overhanging the whole channel, arms dangling, two of them dropping clover petals onto passing hulls for luck, one fae hanging entirely upside-down by her knees and losing a leaf-cloth shoe into the current.

Up in a tall fern above the bank, eight fae in moss-velvet and leaf-cloth jostling for position on a single frond, the frond bowing terrifyingly, one fae pressed against the stem holding everyone else's hazelnuts for safekeeping while chaos builds behind her.

A single fae in scarlet petal-silk balanced on a lone river pebble standing in mid-channel like a grey cliff above the fleet, arms wheeling, clearly about to fall, a dragonfly hovering at eye level as though deciding whether to catch her.

Fae in woven-grass tunics packed onto a broad floating oak leaf drifting slowly downstream, most of them shouting upstream at a race already past, one bailing the leaf with an acorn cap as water ships quietly over the stern edge.

Along the near bank a straggle of fae in plum and marigold petal-silk waving both arms at once, one sliding down the clay bank on a moss patch and arriving in the water still cheering, a water-vole hauled up on a root regarding her without pity.

Four fae in leaf-cloth perched on a watercress strand crossing the channel like a low bridge, bouncing, one tipping backward off it with a shriek and grabbing an ankle at the last moment, a duckling passing underneath with vast indifference.

Fae in moss-velvet clustered on a half-submerged root, two holding a fern frond up over themselves like a sunshade, a third with her ear pressed to the water listening for hull-sound, a fat frog below sitting perfectly still through all of it.

A kingfisher on the tip of a fallen willow branch over the far bend, utterly still, and under it twelve fae in scarlet and copper leaf-cloth running the branch's length, shaking it badly, oblivious to the kingfisher's contempt.

Six fae in birch-bark cloaks and petal-silk riding dragonfly escort in a tight ring above the leaders, one losing her grip and swinging by one hand beneath a wing, her moss-velvet hat spiralling down into the wake below.

Fae in cream and berry-red grass-weave pressed along the underside of an overhanging root, clinging like bats, all craning necks to watch upside-down, one dropping a hazelnut bet that lands precisely in a passing hull and is immediately claimed as ballast.

Three fae in marigold petal-silk standing on a single floating acorn cap in the shallows, the cap shipping water fast, two bailing and one still betting pebbles on the outcome, a newt nosing the cap's rim with scientific interest.

A heron motionless over the far bend like a grey cliff with ideas, and below it along the bank four fae in moss-velvet have tied a strand of plaited grass between two reeds and are arguing furiously about whether the lead hull crossed it first.

Eight fae in leaf-cloth packed onto a mossy boulder mid-stream, one holding up a fern frond to shade her eyes and giving everyone else wrong information, a second fae already in the water behind the boulder where the bank gave way under her boots of acorn-bark.

Fae in woven-grass and petal-silk running along the low root level with the bend, one pressing a polished pebble into another's hand as a losing bet paid mid-sprint without breaking stride, a water-vole watching from further along, unmoved.

Two fae in moss-velvet crouched on a half-submerged stone in the middle of the shallows, one reaching a fern frond out to fend a hull off the stone and accidentally fending it into the lead, the other covering her eyes with her leaf-cloth sleeve.

A loose crowd of fae in scarlet and plum petal-silk up in the fern bank above the course, some lying on their fronts at the frond edge, some swinging their legs, one fae lying on her back watching the sky, having bet on the first hull to swamp.

Fae in birch-bark and moss-velvet clustered on a fallen branch that grazes the water's surface, legs trailing in the current, one fae dragged slowly off the end by the flow still clutching a hazelnut, a dragonfly landing where she sat immediately after.
